patient.chief_complaint: Sudden loss of consciousness at home with brief convulsive movements; found unresponsive by husband
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Eleanor Hartley is a 42-year-old Caucasian woman, a middle school science teacher, who presents to the emergency department via EMS after her husband called 911 when he found her unresponsive on the kitchen floor. According to her husband, she had been eating breakfast and stood up from the table when she suddenly lost consciousness and fell sideways to the floor. She did not call out or appear to have any warning. He observed brief rhythmic movements of her arms and legs lasting approximately 8-10 seconds before she became still. She did not appear cyanotic during the event. She was unresponsive for approximately 25-30 seconds in total, then became aware, looked confused for 10-15 seconds, then asked 'did I fall?' She was immediately oriented and conversational and denied any focal neurological symptoms. EMS arrived 6 minutes later and documented a heart rate of 36-38 bpm with an irregular rhythm on the cardiac monitor. Blood glucose on scene was 94 mg/dL. EMS administered 1 mg atropine IV with a transient increase in heart rate to 58 bpm that was not sustained. She was transported to the ED with a pacing-ready external defibrillator in place.

The patient herself reports that over the past two months she has experienced three episodes of lightheadedness and near-presyncope with position change from sitting to standing, each resolving within 30-60 seconds. She did not seek care, attributing these to her anxiety and possible dehydration. She also endorses progressive fatigue, mild exertional dyspnea (worse over the past 6 weeks), and a dry cough that she assumed was related to her asthma. She denies chest pain, sustained palpitations, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Of note, she was evaluated by her optometrist approximately 6 weeks ago for bilateral blurry vision and photophobia and was told she had bilateral anterior uveitis of unknown cause; an ophthalmology referral was placed but the appointment had not yet occurred.

Her husband endorses that she has seemed 'unusually tired' for the past 2 months and reports she has had intermittent arthralgias in her hands and knees without swelling. She has a maternal aunt with diagnosed pulmonary sarcoidosis.

Her anxiety disorder history had been previously discussed with her primary care physician as a potential cause of her palpitations and fatigue, and she was reassured that her symptoms were likely anxiety-related at a visit 5 weeks ago. She was not started on any new medications at that visit.

results.title: 2017 HRS Expert Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Management of Arrhythmias Associated with Cardiac Sarcoidosis
results.key_finding: Cardiac sarcoidosis should be considered in any patient under 60 years with unexplained complete AV block, sustained VT, or unexplained cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation (endomyocardial biopsy or extracardiac biopsy with compatible cardiac imaging). FDG-PET with adequate dietary preparation and cardiac MRI with LGE are the recommended imaging modalities. Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for high-grade AV block; ICD is considered for documented sustained VT or high-risk features. Corticosteroids are first-line immunosuppressive therapy.

results.title: Diagnostic performance of FDG-PET in cardiac sarcoidosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
results.key_finding: 18F-FDG PET demonstrates sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 78% for active cardiac sarcoidosis when adequate myocardial dietary preparation is achieved. Patchy, non-ischemic focal FDG uptake in the myocardium, particularly in the septal and basal distribution, is the characteristic pattern. Concurrent hilar lymph node FDG uptake supports systemic sarcoidosis.

results.title: Serum ACE level in cardiac sarcoidosis: a diagnostic pitfall
results.key_finding: Serum ACE is normal in up to 40-50% of patients with confirmed cardiac sarcoidosis, including those with isolated or predominant cardiac involvement. A normal ACE level does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis and should not be used as a screening test. ACE sensitivity in systemic sarcoidosis is approximately 57% overall.

output.summary: Cardiac sarcoidosis is an important cause of high-grade AV block and ventricular arrhythmias in adults under 60, with published guidelines (2017 HRS Expert Consensus) recommending a multimodal diagnostic approach combining cardiac MRI and FDG-PET. A normal serum ACE level is insufficient to exclude the diagnosis. Pacemaker implantation is indicated for high-grade AV block; ICD is considered for ventricular arrhythmias or high-risk features. Published registry data support corticosteroid-based immunosuppression to reduce arrhythmia burden and prevent disease progression.

output.proposed: Prednisone 40 mg daily + albuterol PRN (current) in cardiac sarcoidosis with complete AV block and NSVT
interactions: Prednisone + albuterol: Both agents can cause hypokalemia. Monitor serum potassium, particularly given concurrent corticosteroid and beta-2 agonist use. Risk is low at PRN albuterol dosing.
Prednisone: May increase blood glucose; monitor for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, particularly in the context of subclinical thyroid abnormality.

Vitamin D3 (current): Sarcoidosis is associated with hypercalcemia due to extrarenal calcitriol production by granulomas; vitamin D3 supplementation may worsen hypercalcemia risk. Monitor serum calcium closely during corticosteroid therapy — calcium will typically normalize with treatment but supplementation should be re-evaluated.

Albuterol (PRN): Beta-2 agonists may theoretically increase heart rate and trigger arrhythmias in the setting of underlying conduction disease and NSVT; use with caution and reassess asthma management.
contraindications: No absolute contraindications to prednisone in this patient
Avoid high-dose vitamin D3 supplementation until hypercalcemia risk is assessed and serum calcium is monitored under steroid therapy
warnings: Monitor serum calcium: sarcoid granulomas produce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) independently of PTH regulation; concurrent vitamin D3 supplementation may exacerbate hypercalcemia
Monitor potassium with combined prednisone and albuterol use

contraindicated_actions: Do not discharge patient home with complete AV block without temporary pacing protection and definitive device plan
Do not interpret a normal serum ACE level as excluding cardiac sarcoidosis — ACE is normal in up to 50% of confirmed cases
Do not start antiepileptic drugs based on witnessed convulsive movements — these represent convulsive syncope from AV block-mediated cerebral hypoperfusion
Do not perform tilt-table testing — complete AV block is confirmed on resting ECG and tilt-table is not indicated
Do not attribute complete AV block to the borderline-low TSH — thyroid disease does not cause high-grade AV block
key_reasoning_points: Complete AV block in a patient under 60 without prior cardiac disease is cardiac sarcoidosis until proven otherwise and mandates an inflammatory/infiltrative workup
A normal serum ACE level does NOT exclude cardiac sarcoidosis — sensitivity is only ~57% in systemic disease and lower in isolated cardiac involvement
The combination of bilateral uveitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, a family history of sarcoidosis, and pulmonary symptoms constitutes a high-probability systemic sarcoid picture even before imaging

FDG-PET with proper dietary preparation is the imaging modality of choice for active cardiac sarcoidosis; the patchy non-ischemic septal distribution plus hilar lymph node FDG avidity is characteristic
Witnessed convulsive movements during a syncopal episode represent convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion, not an epileptic seizure — the ECG rhythm is the decisive diagnostic finding
Vitamin D3 supplementation must be reassessed in any patient with sarcoidosis given the risk of granuloma-mediated ectopic calcitriol production and hypercalcemia

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: ACE sensitivity in sarcoidosis is approximately 57% overall and lower in isolated cardiac disease; a normal ACE does not exclude the diagnosis and should not redirect workup away from sarcoidosis.

metadata.condition_name: Cardiac syncope (Cardiac Sarcoidosis with Complete AV Block)
metadata.subtype: confirmed cardiac syncope — cardiac sarcoidosis with complete AV block and NSVT
metadata.diagnostic_trap: Normal serum ACE level in a patient with confirmed cardiac sarcoidosis; borderline-low TSH as an alternative distractor; prior psychiatric label deflecting the workup from cardiac disease
clinical_pearls: Cardiac sarcoidosis is a leading cause of high-grade AV block in adults under 60 and should always be considered in unexplained complete AV block in this age group
Serum ACE is normal in up to 40-50% of patients with confirmed cardiac sarcoidosis and should not be used to exclude the diagnosis
The diagnostic triad of uveitis, pulmonary infiltrates/lymphadenopathy, and parotid enlargement (Heerfordt syndrome) can accompany cardiac sarcoidosis — isolated cardiac involvement also occurs

FDG-PET with adequate dietary suppression of physiological myocardial glucose uptake is the preferred imaging modality for active cardiac inflammation in sarcoidosis; patchy non-ischemic septal uptake plus hilar lymph node avidity is the classic pattern
Sarcoidosis granulomas produce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D independently of PTH, leading to hypercalcemia risk that is exacerbated by vitamin D supplementation
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools including FDG-PET as the pivotal imaging step; three embedded red herrings (normal ACE, borderline-low TSH, anxiety history); the ECG is diagnostic but the etiology of complete AV block in a young adult requires extensive multi-modal workup; the normal ACE level creates a strong false-exclusion trap for the naive agent.
citation_gap: HRS 2017 Expert Consensus Statement on Cardiac Sarcoidosis (Birnie DH et al., Heart Rhythm 2014 — precursor; updated 2017) is the canonical guideline for cardiac sarcoidosis diagnosis and management but is not in the SYNC-CARD criteria pack citation allow-list. It is the most directly applicable guideline for FDG-PET recommendation and ICD/pacemaker indications in sarcoid. Cited via ACC_AHA_HRS_2017 and EGSYS_2008 as best available approximations. Recommend adding [HRS_SARCOID_2017] to the SYNC-CARD pack.
